blocks.title: The past, in more than one shape
blocks.subtitle: Describing what used to be, and saying what has just happened.

lessons.title: The imperfect
lessons.subtitle: How things used to be, and what was going on.
lessons.grammarPointEn: imperfect indicative for description, habit and background, contrasted with the periphrastic past for completed events

slides.title: Two pasts, two jobs
slides.body: The periphrastic past says what happened once. The imperfect describes how things were, or what used to happen again and again.

examples.en: I used to eat bread every day.

slides.title: The endings are very regular
slides.body: -ar verbs take -ava; -er, -re and -ir verbs take -ia. A handful build the imperfect on an older stem and simply have to be learnt: ser, fer, veure, dir and dur.

examples.en: As a child I spoke Catalan.
I had a lot of work.

slides.title: Use it to set the scene
slides.body: The imperfect paints the background; the periphrastic past drops the event into it.

examples.target: Plovia i vaig tornar a casa.
examples.en: It was raining and I went back home.

examples.target: Eren les vuit quan va arribar.
examples.en: It was eight o'clock when he arrived.

exercises.en: As a child I used to read a lot.
The house was very big.
He used to make dinner every night.

exercises.target: Nosaltres ___ a la platja cada estiu.
exercises.en: We used to go to the beach every summer.
I had a small dog.

exercises.target: Cada dia vaig menjar a casa.
exercises.en: Every day I used to eat at home.
exercises.hint: A repeated habit takes the imperfect.

exercises.prompt: Match each verb with its imperfect.

exercises.en: I used to work in the city.
distractorsEn: I worked in the city once.
I work in the city.
I will work in the city.

lessons.title: The perfect with haver
lessons.subtitle: For what has happened today.
lessons.grammarPointEn: the perfect: present of haver plus the past participle, used for events inside a period that is still running

slides.title: haver plus the participle
slides.body: Use it for something that happened inside a stretch of time that is still going, above all today. For yesterday, use the periphrastic past.

examples.en: Today we have worked a lot.

slides.title: Participles, regular and not
slides.body: -ar gives -at, -er and -re give -ut, -ir gives -it. A handful are irregular and worth memorising outright.

slides.title: Never split haver from its participle
slides.body: Nothing goes between them. Adverbs come after the participle, or before haver.

exercises.en: Today I have eaten a lot.
She has opened the door.
We have arrived late.
Have you seen the book?
They have made dinner.
Yesterday I ate fish.
exercises.hint: Yesterday is over, so use the periphrastic past.

exercises.prompt: Match each verb with its participle.

exercises.en: I have spoken with the doctor.
distractorsEn: I speak with the doctor.
I will speak with the doctor.
I used to speak with the doctor.

lessons.title: Reflexive verbs
lessons.subtitle: The everyday verbs that carry a pronoun with them.
lessons.grammarPointEn: reflexive verbs with em/et/es/ens/us/es, their daily-routine vocabulary, and the reciprocal use

slides.title: The pronoun changes with the person
slides.body: The dictionary lists the verb with -se on the end. In use, that -se becomes em, et, es, ens or us, and moves in front of the verb.

slides.title: The daily routine is built from them
slides.body: Most of what you do in a morning is a reflexive verb in Catalan.

slides.title: The same forms say "each other"
slides.body: In the plural, the reflexive often means the action goes both ways.

examples.en: We see each other every day.
They know each other very well.

exercises.en: My name is Marta.
His name is Joan.
We get up at seven.
Every morning I shower.
My name is Anna.

exercises.prompt: Match the reflexive verb with its meaning.

exercises.en: I get up at seven every day.
We see each other every Saturday.
distractorsEn: I see them every Saturday.
They see us every Saturday.
We saw each other on Saturday.

blocks.title: The small words that carry the sentence
blocks.subtitle: Weak pronouns - the part of Catalan that has no English equivalent.

lessons.title: Object pronouns
lessons.subtitle: el, la, els, les, li - and where they sit.
lessons.grammarPointEn: direct object pronouns el/la/els/les and indirect li/els, their position before the conjugated verb, and enclitic attachment to infinitives and imperatives

slides.title: They go before the verb
slides.body: Unlike English, the object pronoun comes in front of the conjugated verb, not after it.

slides.title: el and la shrink to l' before a vowel
slides.body: Exactly like the article. la stays whole before an unstressed i- or u-.

examples.en: I listen to it every morning.

slides.title: li is for the person you give something to
slides.body: Use li when English would say "to him" or "to her", even when English leaves the "to" out.

examples.en: I write to her every week.

slides.title: After an infinitive they hook on with a hyphen
slides.body: When the verb is an infinitive or an imperative, the pronoun goes on the end instead.

exercises.en: I see him every day.

exercises.target: ___ dono el llibre a la Marta.
exercises.en: I give the book to Marta.
I have seen him today.
I want to see it tomorrow.
The apples? I buy them at the market.
I see him every day.

exercises.prompt: Match each pronoun with what it stands for.

exercises.en: I write to her every week.
distractorsEn: She writes to me every week.
I read it every week.
I see her every week.

lessons.title: hi and en
lessons.subtitle: Two pronouns English simply does not have.
lessons.grammarPointEn: hi replaces a place or a prepositional phrase; en replaces a quantity or a de-phrase and is obligatory where English drops it

slides.title: hi stands for a place
slides.body: Where English repeats the place, or just says "there", Catalan uses hi. It is also the hi inside hi ha.

examples.target: Vas a la platja? Sí, hi vaig.
examples.en: Are you going to the beach? Yes, I'm going.
There are a lot of people.

slides.title: en stands for a quantity or a de-phrase
slides.body: When you say how many, Catalan keeps en in the sentence. English drops it entirely, which is why it is easy to forget.

examples.en: Do you want bread? Yes, I want some.

slides.title: They shorten too
slides.body: en becomes n' before a vowel, and 'n after one.

exercises.en: There are a lot of people in the street.
Do you want water? Yes, I want some.
Are you going to school? Yes, I'm going.
I have three of them.
There are four of them.
Do you want bread? Yes, I want some.
exercises.hint: Catalan keeps en even though English drops it.

exercises.target: Hi ha un gos al parc.
exercises.en: There is a dog in the park.
distractorsEn: The dog is in the park.
He has a dog in the park.
There was a dog in the park.

exercises.en: I want two of them.
distractorsEn: I want it twice.
There are two.
I have two.

lessons.title: m'agrada
lessons.subtitle: The verb that turns the sentence around.
lessons.grammarPointEn: agradar and verbs like it: the thing liked is the grammatical subject, so the verb agrees with it and the person takes a weak pronoun

slides.title: The thing you like is the subject
slides.body: Catalan says something closer to "coffee pleases me". So the verb agrees with the thing, not with you.

slides.title: Only the pronoun changes for the person
slides.body: em, et, li, ens, us, els - the same weak pronouns, with the vowel forms m' and t' before agrada.

slides.title: A few more verbs work the same way
slides.body: Once you have agradar, these come free.

exercises.en: I like coffee.
I like books.
Marta likes reading.
We like this house.
My head hurts.
I like books.
exercises.hint: The verb agrees with the books.

exercises.en: I like this house a lot.
Do you like films?
distractorsEn: Do you like the film?
Did you like the films?
Do the films please you today?

blocks.title: Looking forward, and comparing
blocks.subtitle: The future, being polite, and putting things side by side.

lessons.title: The future
lessons.subtitle: Built on the infinitive, so it is almost free.
lessons.grammarPointEn: the future built on the full infinitive, with the shortened stems of the common irregular verbs

slides.title: Add the endings to the whole infinitive
slides.body: The endings are the same for all three conjugations, so there is only one set to learn.

slides.title: A few stems shorten
slides.body: The most common verbs lose a syllable, but the endings never change.

slides.title: For something about to happen
slides.body: Catalan does not use anar a + infinitive for the future the way Spanish uses ir a - that is a calque, and va menjar already means "he ate". Use the future tense, or estar a punt de for imminence.

examples.target: Ara estic a punt de menjar.

exercises.en: Tomorrow I'll go to the beach.
I'll have time next week.
They will arrive tomorrow morning.
We will make dinner.
She will be able to come on Saturday.
Tomorrow I'll have a lot of work.

exercises.prompt: Match each verb with its future stem.

exercises.en: I will go to Girona on Monday.
distractorsEn: I go to Girona on Mondays.
I went to Girona on Monday.
I would go to Girona on Monday.

lessons.title: The conditional
lessons.subtitle: How to ask for things without sounding blunt.
lessons.grammarPointEn: the conditional on the future stem, used for politeness, hypothesis and softened requests

slides.title: Same stem as the future, imperfect endings
slides.body: If you know the future, the conditional costs you nothing new.

slides.title: This is how you are polite in a shop
slides.body: vull sounds abrupt. voldria and m'agradaria are what people actually say.

examples.en: I would like a glass of water.
Could you tell me the time?

slides.title: And for what you would do
slides.body: Use it for a situation that is imagined rather than real.

examples.en: I would go to the beach.

exercises.en: I would like a coffee, please.
Could you help me?
I would like to go to the beach.
It would be better tomorrow morning.
We would eat at home.

exercises.target: Vull un got d'aigua, si us plau.
exercises.en: I would like a glass of water, please.
exercises.hint: The conditional is what makes it polite.
exercises.correctedTarget: Voldria un got d'aigua, si us plau.

exercises.prompt: Match the future with its conditional.

exercises.en: I would like to speak with the doctor.
distractorsEn: I like speaking with the doctor.
I will speak with the doctor.
I liked speaking with the doctor.

lessons.title: Comparing things
lessons.subtitle: més, menys, tan - and the two irregulars.
lessons.grammarPointEn: comparatives with més/menys ... que, equality with tan/tant ... com, superlatives with the article, and the irregulars millor and pitjor

slides.title: More, less, as
slides.body: Catalan builds comparisons with separate words. There is nothing like the English -er ending.

examples.target: La casa és més gran que l'escola.
examples.en: The house is bigger than the school.

examples.target: És tan alt com el seu pare.
examples.en: He is as tall as his father.

slides.title: tan before an adjective, tant with a noun or verb
slides.body: One letter apart, and it is the commonest slip at this level.

examples.en: He is as big as me.
I work as much as you.

slides.title: The superlative just adds the article
slides.body: Put el, la, els or les in front of més, and use de where English says "in".

examples.target: És el més gran de la família.
examples.en: He is the oldest in the family.

examples.target: La ciutat més bonica del país.
examples.en: The most beautiful city in the country.

slides.title: Two irregulars
slides.body: bo and dolent have their own comparative forms, exactly like English good and bad.

exercises.target: La casa és ___ gran que l'escola.
exercises.en: The house is bigger than the school.

exercises.target: És tan alt ___ el seu pare.
exercises.en: He is as tall as his father.
This coffee is better than the other.
He is the biggest of all.
I work as much as you.
He is as tall as me.
exercises.hint: Before an adjective it loses the -t.

exercises.en: My house is smaller than yours.

exercises.target: És la ciutat més bonica del país.
exercises.en: It is the most beautiful city in the country.
distractorsEn: It is a beautiful city in the country.
The city is more beautiful than the country.
It is as beautiful as the country.

lessons.title: Joining sentences
lessons.subtitle: però, perquè, quan, mentre - and the que that does everything.
lessons.grammarPointEn: coordinating and subordinating connectors, and relative clauses with que, qui and on

slides.title: The connectors you will use every day
slides.body: Catalan writes perquè as one word both for "because" and for "so that"; the question word per què is two.

examples.en: I want to go out, but it's raining.
I'm not coming because I'm tired.
When I arrive, I'll call you.

slides.title: que links a clause to a noun
slides.body: Where English can drop "that", Catalan never does.

examples.target: El llibre que llegeixo és bo.
examples.en: The book I'm reading is good.

examples.target: La casa on visc és petita.
examples.en: The house where I live is small.

slides.title: qui only for people, after a preposition
slides.body: For a person as the plain subject or object, que is still the normal choice.

exercises.en: I want to go out, but it's raining.
I'm not coming because I'm tired.
I listen to music while I work.

exercises.target: El llibre ___ llegeixo és molt bo.
exercises.en: The book I'm reading is very good.
The house where I live is small.

exercises.target: La dona qui treballa aquí és la Marta.
exercises.en: The woman who works here is Marta.
exercises.hint: qui needs a preposition in front of it.
exercises.correctedTarget: La dona que treballa aquí és la Marta.

exercises.prompt: Match the connector with its meaning.

exercises.target: No surto perquè fa molt fred.
exercises.en: I'm not going out because it's very cold.
distractorsEn: I go out although it's very cold.
I'm not going out, but it's very cold.
Why am I not going out in the cold?

blocks.title: Rounding out A2
blocks.subtitle: The subjunctive, the gerund, and pronouns that combine.

lessons.title: The present subjunctive
lessons.subtitle: For what you want, hope or need to happen.
lessons.grammarPointEn: the present subjunctive after voler que, esperar que and cal que, and after quan with future reference

slides.title: The endings swap over
slides.body: -ar verbs take the -i endings; -er, -re and -ir verbs take them too. The vowel that marked the conjugation simply changes.

examples.en: I want you to speak Catalan.

table: parli, parlis, parli, parlem, parleu, parlin
perdi, perdis, perdi, perdem, perdeu, perdin
dormi, dormis, dormi, dormim, dormiu, dormin
serveixi, serveixis, serveixi, servim, serviu, serveixin

slides.title: The irregulars build on the -c stem
slides.body: If you remember tinc, vinc and puc, you already have the subjunctive: add -gui.

examples.en: I want you to have time.

slides.title: What triggers it
slides.body: A wish, a need, an emotion - and quan when it points at the future, where English keeps the present.

exercises.en: I want you to speak Catalan.
I hope he arrives soon.
You need to come tomorrow morning.

exercises.target: Vull que ___ temps per a tu.
exercises.en: I want you to have time for yourself.
I hope it's a good night.
I want you to come tomorrow.

exercises.prompt: Match each verb with its subjunctive.

exercises.en: You need to study every day.
distractorsEn: You study every day.
You will study every day.
You used to study every day.

lessons.title: The gerund, impersonal es, and periphrases
lessons.subtitle: Three structures that make you sound fluent.
lessons.grammarPointEn: the gerund for simultaneity only, the impersonal es, and the verbal periphrases haver de, tornar a and acabar de

slides.title: The gerund is for two things at once
slides.body: -ar gives -ant, -er and -re give -ent, -ir gives -int. Use it only when the two actions overlap - never for one thing after another.

examples.en: I listen to music while working.

examples.target: Va caure i es va trencar el braç.
examples.en: He fell and broke his arm.

slides.title: es for when nobody in particular does it
slides.body: This is how Catalan says "one", "people" or a passive. The verb agrees with the thing.

slides.title: Verb plus verb
slides.body: These carry a lot of everyday meaning that English packs into single words like "must" or "just".

exercises.en: I'm making dinner now.
Catalan is spoken here.
I have to work tomorrow.
I have just arrived home.
I'm reading the book again.
I have to work tomorrow.
exercises.hint: Obligation uses haver de, not tenir.

exercises.prompt: Match the periphrasis with its meaning.

exercises.en: I have just seen Marta.
distractorsEn: I finish watching Marta.
I am going to see Marta.
I saw Marta a long time ago.

lessons.title: Pronouns that combine
lessons.subtitle: me'l, se'n, l'hi - the apostrophes finally make sense.
lessons.grammarPointEn: combining two weak pronouns, their four written shapes, and enclitic attachment to infinitives and imperatives

slides.title: Every weak pronoun has four shapes
slides.body: Which one you write depends on what is next to it: a consonant, a vowel, or another pronoun. em is the model for et and es.

slides.title: Two pronouns together
slides.body: The order is fixed by form, not by meaning: a 1st or 2nd person pronoun comes before a 3rd person one (me'l, te'n), and en and ho come last. With li the two fuse into l'hi.

examples.en: He'll give it to me tomorrow.
I'll talk to you about it later.

slides.title: After the verb they hook on with a hyphen
slides.body: With an infinitive or an imperative the pronouns move to the end and keep the same order.

examples.en: I want to tell you now.

exercises.en: The book? He'll give it to me tomorrow.
He goes off home early.
I want to tell you right now.
He helps me a lot every day.
He wants to help me with the work.

exercises.target: Vol ajudar em amb la feina.
exercises.en: He wants to help me with the work.
exercises.hint: After an infinitive the pronoun hooks on.

exercises.prompt: Match the combination with its written form.

exercises.en: I left very early.
distractorsEn: I arrived very early.
I want to go very early.
He left me very early.
